units.name: Classifying Matter
units.summary: Elements, compounds and mixtures, and how they differ.

topics.name: Elements, Compounds and Mixtures
topics.summary: Three kinds of substance, and how to tell them apart.

objectives.text: Classify a substance into one of the three.
Explain why a compound differs from a mixture of the same elements.

keyTerms.definition: A substance made of only one kind of atom.
Two or more elements chemically joined in fixed proportions.
Substances together but not chemically joined.

sections.heading: What you will learn
sections.body: Everything around you is one of three kinds of substance. Telling them apart is the foundation of chemistry, and the compound-versus-mixture distinction is the one that does the most work later.

sections.heading: The three kinds
sections.body:
ELEMENT — made of only ONE kind of atom. It cannot be broken into anything simpler by chemical means.

    oxygen, iron, carbon, gold

COMPOUND — two or more elements CHEMICALLY JOINED, always in the same proportions.

    water (H₂O) — hydrogen and oxygen, always 2 to 1
    salt (NaCl) — sodium and chlorine, always 1 to 1

MIXTURE — substances together but NOT chemically joined. The proportions can be anything.

    air, sea water, soil, rice mixed with beans

sections.heading: Compound versus mixture
sections.body:
This is the distinction that matters, so take it slowly. There are three differences.

**1. Are they joined?**
In a compound the atoms are chemically bonded. In a mixture they are only sitting together.

**2. Fixed proportions?**
Water is ALWAYS 2 hydrogen to 1 oxygen. Never 3 to 1. A mixture has no fixed recipe — tea can be weak or strong and is still tea.

**3. Can you separate it easily?**
A mixture can be separated physically — filtering, evaporating, picking out by hand. A compound needs a chemical reaction.

And the consequence that surprises people: **a compound has completely different properties from the elements in it.**
sections.example:
Sodium, chlorine, and salt.

SODIUM on its own is a soft metal that reacts violently with water.
CHLORINE on its own is a poisonous green gas.

Join them chemically and you get SODIUM CHLORIDE — ordinary table salt, which you eat every day.

A dangerous metal plus a poisonous gas makes something safe and necessary. That is not a mixture behaving like its parts; it is a new substance.

Now compare with a MIXTURE. Mix iron filings with sulfur powder. It still looks like iron filings and sulfur, and a magnet pulls the iron straight back out — because nothing joined.

Heat that same mixture, and the elements react to form iron sulfide. Now the magnet does nothing. A compound has formed, and the properties changed.

sections.heading: Classifying quickly
sections.body:
Ask in this order:

1. Is it one kind of atom only? → ELEMENT
2. Are different elements chemically joined in fixed proportions? → COMPOUND
3. Are different substances just together, separable physically? → MIXTURE

A warning: a chemical FORMULA tells you it is a compound, not a mixture. H₂O is a compound. "Salt water" has no single formula — it is salt (a compound) mixed with water (a compound), so the whole thing is a mixture.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
sections.body:
Element, compound or mixture?
1. Copper
2. Carbon dioxide (CO₂)
3. Sea water
4. Air
5. Sugar (C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁)

Then: explain why salt is safe to eat although sodium and chlorine are both dangerous.
And: how could you separate salt from sea water? Does that tell you it is a mixture?

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body:
• Element: one kind of atom.
• Compound: elements chemically joined, fixed proportions, new properties.
• Mixture: substances together, any proportions, physically separable.
• A compound behaves nothing like the elements it contains.
• A formula means compound; no single formula usually means mixture.

questions.question: Which of these is a compound?
questions.explanation: Water (H₂O) is hydrogen and oxygen chemically joined in fixed proportions — always 2 to 1. Oxygen and iron are elements, one kind of atom each. Air is a mixture of gases that are not chemically joined.

questions.question: Sodium reacts violently with water and chlorine is a poisonous gas, yet sodium chloride is safe to eat. Why?
options: The dangerous parts are removed during the reaction
A compound is a new substance with its own properties, not a mixture of its elements
Salt contains only a tiny amount of each
Sodium and chlorine are not really dangerous
questions.explanation: When elements bond chemically they form a NEW substance whose properties need not resemble theirs at all. Nothing is removed and no element is present in its free form. This is the clearest difference from a mixture, where each part keeps its own behaviour.

questions.question: Which is the best evidence that sea water is a MIXTURE rather than a compound?
options: The salt can be separated out by evaporating the water
It contains more than one element
questions.explanation: A mixture can be separated by physical means such as evaporation; a compound needs a chemical reaction. Containing several elements is not enough on its own — water itself contains two and is a compound.
